source: Frischkorn & Oberauer (2021) Intelligence test items varying in capacity demands cannot be used to test the capacity hypothesis
finding: Simulated three formal versions of the capacity hypothesis. Almost any pattern of item-WMC correlation across capacity demand can arise. So 'correlation grows with demand' is not implied by the hypothesis.
numbers: Three models; item-WMC correlation depends on (1) share of ability variance from WMC and (2) match of item demand to sample mean WMC.
quote: The capacity hypothesis does not imply stronger correlations of WMC and intelligence test items with higher capacity demands.
limits: Simulation only; other implementations of the hypothesis exist. A logic critique, not data.
agent_relevance: Item difficulty or rule count is not a clean proxy for capacity load. Our agent must measure load directly, not assume it from rule count.

source: Frischkorn & Oberauer (2021) Discussion: why demand-based tests fail
finding: Prior supporting studies (Salthouse 1993, Unsworth & Engle 2005, Wiley 2011, Little 2014, Burgoyne 2019) assumed a prediction the hypothesis does not make. Converges with Smolen & Chuderski's statistical critique.
numbers: Pattern depends on WMC share of ability variance and on match of demand to sample mean WMC.
limits: Authors say other model versions could differ.
agent_relevance: Evidence for 'capacity matters' must come from manipulating load directly, as the n-back and REL studies do.

source: Dokic, Koso-Drljevic, Bilalic (2025) Past reflections, present insights: WMC-Gf systematic review and new empirical research
finding: Review found inconsistent methods and mixed evidence. New study (item difficulty analysis, rule-token analysis, SEM, latent growth curves) found no support for the capacity account.
numbers: N=543; WMC = Operation, Reading, Symmetry span; Gf = Raven APM items. Intelligence 108, art. 101874.
quote: We could not confirm the capacity hypothesis either when we employed ... Raven's item difficulty or ... rule tokens.
limits: Read from the publisher portal abstract page only, not the full paper. A few studies (Little 2014) did find the effect. Frischkorn & Oberauer argue the test itself is weak.
agent_relevance: Do not assume rule count alone drives difficulty. Measure per-item load and failure empirically.

source: Smolen & Chuderski (2015) Quadratic relationship between item difficulty and correlation with working memory
finding: Item-WM correlation is not linear in difficulty. It rises then falls (inverted U) on Raven items, driven by floor and ceiling effects.
numbers: Raven 36 items; N=347 and N=939. Linear fit F(1,34)=0.4, p=.53. Quadratic adj R2 .14 (N=347), .23 (N=939). Breakpoint error rate .44 / .42. Slopes r=+.46/+.53 before, -.52/-.50 after. New vs old rule items z=1.41, p=.17.
limits: Two samples from one lab (Chuderski). Correlational.
agent_relevance: A linear 'harder means more capacity' model of our agent's failures would misfit. Expect non-monotone relations.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better
finding: Positive result for the capacity hypothesis: WMC matters more on harder Raven items and on items with more rule tokens, but only when the overall WMC-Raven correlation is moderate to high.
numbers: N=126 students. Composite WMC r=.56 with Raven: item-wise slope .004, t(34)=2.87, p<.01, R2=.20. OSPAN alone r=.36: slope n.s. (t(34)=1.39). Rule tokens: beta=-0.10 on accuracy, WMC x tokens p<.01. Simulated slopes .0002 (rho=.10) to .0016 (rho=.90).
limits: Small N; Wiley et al. found no token effect over 1-4 tokens (r about .33). Dokic 2025 did not replicate.
agent_relevance: The effect is fragile and measure-dependent. A claim from one benchmark may not carry over.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Digit Matrices)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) solved text Raven-style Digit Matrices zero-shot at or above human level. Its difficulty pattern across problem types resembled humans (one-, two-, three-rule, logic).
numbers: Humans N=40 UCLA students. Generative accuracy GPT-3 over humans OR=1.88, p=.005, CI [1.21,2.91]. Multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8. Profile correlation with humans r(30)=.39, p=.027. Problem type effect OR=0.5. In three-rule problems accuracy depended on number of unique rules, holding total rules fixed.
limits: Older model; text digits remove perception. Contamination debated. Rule count was confounded with progression rules, which were harder (human OR=.41, p=.0001).
agent_relevance: Rule count matters but unique-rule count and rule type matter too. Template for an item-level difficulty model.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Digit Matrices vs Raven SPM
finding: Human digit-matrix performance matched image-based Raven SPM across one-rule, two-rule and logic types, so digit text matrices are a usable stand-in.
numbers: SPM comparison N=80 (data from earlier study) vs digit matrices N=40; three-rule items have no SPM counterpart.
limits: Validity by profile similarity, not full psychometric equating.
agent_relevance: Text matrices are valid test beds for scaffold ablations.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to Lewis & Mitchell. GPT-4 fails counterfactual letter-string analogies mainly through counting. With code execution it solves them near human level.
numbers: gpt-4-0125-preview, temperature 0; 300 problems at interval size 1. Code-execution GPT-4 did better than plain GPT-4; human vs code GPT-4 P=.496. 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors.
limits: Letter-string task, not matrices. The cause was counting, a sub-skill, not rule load.
agent_relevance: A tool (code) removes a specific bottleneck. Diagnose the failing sub-skill before adding scaffold steps.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: On verbal and spatial n-back, ChatGPT accuracy and d-prime drop as n rises. Authors say capacity is about 3, like humans.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, temperature 1. d-prime falls to about 1 at n=3 in three verbal variants; noise variant lower. Larger spatial grid gave higher capacity. GPT-4 higher than other LLMs on verbal tasks.
quote: ChatGPT has a working memory capacity limit strikingly similar to that of humans.
limits: Challenged by Hu & Lewis 2025 as task misunderstanding. N-back mixes storage and updating.
agent_relevance: A load-vs-performance curve is the right test in an LLM, but needs controls for instruction understanding.

source: Gong et al. (2024) n-back: instruction and noise effects
finding: Capacity pattern persisted across instruction strategies; added noise lowered d-prime and capacity.
numbers: Noise variant d-prime lower at n=3 than other variants; GPT-4 tested on fewer variants because of cost.
limits: Cost-limited GPT-4 testing.
agent_relevance: Distractor content reduces effective capacity. Strip irrelevant context before reasoning steps.

source: Hu & Lewis (2025) Do language models understand the cognitive tasks given to them? N-back paradigm
finding: Poor 2-back and 3-back scores come partly from task misunderstanding: models answer a different m-back task. A strong model reached high accuracy up to 10-back with demos.
numbers: Strong model on 8-, 9-, 10-back: 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75%. Weak models (Qwen 1.5 14B, Llama 3.1 8B) score 1.00 on 1-back but about .09-.20 on 2- and 3-back. GPT-3.5 .51 and .43; Llama 3.1 70B .99 and .93.
quote: these results may reflect the model's failure to understand the task requirements rather than any inherent memory limitation.
limits: Open-source models; interactive demos help; attention analysis on few models.
agent_relevance: Measured failure at load may be task-set drift, not capacity. Re-anchor instructions and verify the task is being followed.

source: Hu & Lewis (2025) n-back: retrieval accuracy by model tier
finding: Models fall in tiers: T1 above 80% on 2- and 3-back, T2 about 50% and 40%, T3 about 20%. Weak models drift to m-back as errors accumulate.
numbers: A mid model's demo-assisted retrievals consistent with the correct task: 75.25%, 66.08%, 57.1%; task accuracies 83.33%, 78.25%, 71.92%.
limits: Open-source models only.
agent_relevance: Early errors change the task set. Re-anchor instructions each step in long loops.

source: Gong & Zhang (2024) Self-attention limits working memory capacity of transformer-based models
finding: Small decoder transformers trained on n-back learn attention to the n-back position. Total attention entropy rises with N, and accuracy falls with entropy.
numbers: Vanilla transformers trained on n-back; performance negatively correlated with total entropy of the attention matrix across N.
limits: Small trained models, not frontier LLMs; mechanism is correlational.
agent_relevance: A mechanism for load limits: attention dilutes as more items must be bound. Keep few items in view per step.

source: Fesser et al. (2026) Evaluating relational reasoning in LLMs with REL (ICML)
finding: Accuracy falls steadily as relational complexity (entities bound at once) rises, with entity count held fixed. Entity count is a noisy proxy for difficulty.
numbers: Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, GPT-5.2. REL-A: -45% as RC rises; REL-B1: -93%; REL-C1 to C3 completion falls 39.7%. Homoplasy: 35% at 4 taxa to 1% at 25. RC explains 24% (Claude), 32% (Gemini), 44% (GPT) of explainable variance; next factor 7%, 17%, 6%.
quote: performance degrades consistently and monotonically as RC increases, even when the total number of entities is held fixed.
limits: Generated tasks in algebra, biology, chemistry; not matrices. Some tasks get easier with more input when RC stays fixed.
agent_relevance: Direct parallel to the capacity test with a measured load variable. Load is binding arity, not rule or token count. Measure it.

source: Fesser et al. (2026) REL: test-time compute and in-context examples
finding: More thinking tokens and one-shot examples do not remove the relational-complexity drop.
numbers: Token cap 4096 to 16384 added about 2-3% on REL-A4/A5; on REL-C average change 0.4%. One-shot ICL helped below 20 molecules, not at high RC. 30x30 RPM (REL-A3): Claude and Gemini about 12%, GPT-5.2 down nearly 40%.
limits: One-shot run on only 10% of REL-C questions.
agent_relevance: Extra compute alone will not fix high-arity binding. Decompose so each step binds fewer things.

source: Fesser et al. (2026) REL: low-RC tasks and fixed-RC larger inputs
finding: Low-RC tasks are near-solved even when large. When RC is fixed, more input helps. High initial RC stays unsolved at any size.
numbers: REL-A1/A2 (RC 1-2): up to 91% on 30x30 matrices. REL-A5: 56-64% rising to 77-87%; REL-A6: 41-50% to 53-64%; REL-A7 (RC 6) about 12% at every size. REL-C1 accuracy 56.0% at 5 molecules to 71.0% at 50.
limits: Synthetic tasks.
agent_relevance: Size is not load. Match test design to actual binding arity. Same lesson as Dokic 2025: the proxy (count) failed, the real variable worked.

source: Patil et al. (2026) Diagnosing algebraic reasoning failures in LLMs across nine complexity dimensions
finding: Varying each factor alone, parallel branch count is a scale-invariant working-memory bottleneck. Seven models fully accurate to 12 branches then collapse between 20 and 30.
numbers: Seven models, 8B to 235B. Branch depth: Llama 3 8B breaks at 3 ops per branch (17%); Claude 3.5 Haiku keeps 20% at 12. Chain length: GPT-4o mini 100% to step 4, 0% from step 5. Claude 3.5 Haiku 100% at counting loads K=5..300.
limits: Under-review preprint; synthetic algebra; older small models.
agent_relevance: Width and depth are separate loads, and the count of items held at once is separable from step count. Keep parallel sub-results under about 12.

source: Patil et al. (2026) multiplication digits (cites Dziri 2024)
finding: Cites GPT-4 falling from 59% on 3-digit to 4% on 4-digit multiplication. Own test: frontier models above 50% through 8 digits, small models collapse at 4, all fail at 15.
numbers: As reported in the paper text.
limits: Dziri et al. cited, not opened.
agent_relevance: Cliffs are task and model specific; calibrate per step.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi, Oh (2026) NeuroCognition: neuropsychologically grounded evaluation of LLM cognitive abilities
finding: Ten multimodal models: text beats image on all three tests (Raven, spatial WM, WCST); harder levels lower scores (p<.001). Humans and LLMs fail at different parts: humans fail to remember, LLMs fail to manipulate.
numbers: Humans RAPM text 0.430 (MC) / 0.444 (Gen), image 0.814 (N=9). SWM humans 0.963 easy, 0.878 hard (N=11). GPT-5 SWM image-hard 0.631 to 0.989 with text added. Factor analysis of 156 LLMs: one factor, 75% variance. NeuroCognition vs 11-benchmark average r=.86, p=.001, N=10.
limits: Human samples tiny (N=9-11). Text RAPM is novel and humans find it hard.
agent_relevance: LLM failure is not human-like capacity. Externalised state (history, notes) removes maintenance load; manipulation is the weak point.

source: Haznitrama et al. (2026) NeuroCognition: prompting ablations
finding: Complex reasoning is not always helpful. Disabling reasoning on RAPM raised text multiple-choice scores for some models. Pattern hints gave no gain in 10 models. Notes helped only marginally.
numbers: RAPM reasoning off (4 models) Text MC p=.021; pattern hints all n.s. (10 models); Claude Sonnet 4 and Grok 4 Fast had reasoning disabled on RAPM because overthinking exhausted output limits. WCST notes image-hard p=.052.
limits: One RAPM run per model; paired t tests on few models.
agent_relevance: Over-long thinking can hurt rule-induction items. Cap thinking and verify.

source: Haznitrama et al. (2026) NeuroCognition: WCST and SWM details
finding: Rule switching (WCST) is easiest for LLMs. Errors appear after the rule is found: failure to maintain set and perseveration. Notes externalise the rule guess.
numbers: SWM with history: humans near ceiling 0.982.
limits: Small human N; marginal significance.
agent_relevance: Keep an explicit rule ledger the agent re-reads.

source: Li (2025) A study of rule omission in Raven's Progressive Matrices (I-RAVEN)
finding: Models trained with one or two rules omitted fail on those rules. Token accuracy hides failure in whole-answer accuracy.
numbers: Seq-seq transformer on omitted rules: 47.00% (one removed), 31.47% (two removed); seen rules 92.62% / 93.42%. CoPINet 30.29% / 16.13%; DCNet 36.43% / 23.93%. Token accuracy 96.88% yet answer accuracy 45.31% (Center).
limits: Student-scale; trained from scratch, not prompted frontier LLMs.
agent_relevance: Rule novelty, not rule count, drives failure. Score complete answers.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Marvelous Agents? MLLMs on abstract reasoning (IQ50, RAVEN-S, CCSE), COLM
finding: Open-source multimodal models near chance on puzzles easy for people. Closed models improved with chain-of-thought demos.
numbers: Humans N=25 college students: 95.9% (SD 6.92) on IQ50. gpt-4v gained as much as 100% with symmetric CoT demos. One-shot raised gpt-4v safeguard triggers 4% to 18%.
limits: 2023-24 models; perception confound.
agent_relevance: Separate perception from reasoning before blaming capacity.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Three regimes by puzzle complexity: plain models better at low, reasoning models better at medium, both collapse at high. Thinking tokens fall near the collapse point.
numbers: Puzzles incl. Tower of Hanoi (disks); Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini.
limits: Disputed by Lawsen: output token limits and unsolvable instances.
agent_relevance: Load curves can be non-monotone in effort. Budget thinking by difficulty.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: Much of the claimed collapse is a design artefact: output token limits, and River Crossing with N>5 and boat capacity 3 is unsolvable. Asking for a generating function fixes Hanoi.
numbers: Preliminary experiments, multiple models.
limits: Short, preliminary comment.
agent_relevance: A failure at high load may be an output-format limit. Test a different output format before concluding capacity.

source: Li et al. (2026) RIDE: IRT-based difficulty evolving perturbation for math reasoning
finding: Uses 35 LLMs as simulated students and a 1PL item response model to rank item difficulty and rewrite questions to be harder.
numbers: 35 LLMs; 1PL IRT difficulty per question.
limits: Math word problems; no working-memory link.
agent_relevance: Method: estimate difficulty from model responses, not from rule counts.

source: Galanti & Baron (2024) Intelligence analysis of language models (ARC)
finding: Open-source LLMs on text-encoded ARC tasks struggle even on simpler subsets; zero-shot then CoT tested.
numbers: Exact scores not extracted.
limits: Student project; small subsets.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence; text encoding of grids is itself a difficulty source.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Raven)
finding: Origin of the capacity hypothesis and the FAIRAVEN/BETTERRAVEN production-system models; described second-hand via Frischkorn & Oberauer.
numbers: Cited only.
quote: two aspects: induce abstract relations; manage larger sets of goals in working memory (paraphrase)
limits: Not opened directly.
agent_relevance: Source of the goal-management idea in our schema.
